  SUBJECT:  AGREEMENT  WITH  JOHN  L. HUNTER  AND  ASSOCIATES,  INC.,  FOR
  THE MANAGEMENT  OF THE INDUSTRIAL  WASTE  PROGRAM  AND  THE  FAT,  OIL,
  AND GREASE  CONTROL  PROGRAM

  PURPOSE:  To approve  a three-year  Agreement  with John L. Hunter  and Associates,  Inc., for
  the management of the City of South Gate's ("City")  Industrial  Waste ("IW")  Program  and the
  Fat, Oil, and Grease ("FOG") Control Program.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council  will  consider:
  a.  Approving  the Agreement  with  John L. Hunter  and Associates,  Inc. ("JLHA"),  for the
  management  of the Industrial  Waste  Program  and the Fat,  Oil,  and Grease  Control
  Program,  for a three-year  term, in an amount not to exceed $194,691;  and
  b.  Authorizing  the Mayor  to execute the Agreement  in a form acceptable to the City Attorney.

  FISCALIMPACT:  ThereisnoimpactontheGeneralFund.TheAgreement,totaling$l94,691,
  will be funded through Sewer Funds. The cost of services is distributed  over three years: $63,000
  in Year 1, $65,000 in Year 2, and $67,000 in Year 3. Year 1 services  are included in the Fiscal
  Year 2025/26 0perating Budget.

  ANALYSIS:  The proposed  Agreement  with  JLHA  ensures continued  compliance  with  state-
  mandated Waste Discharge  Requirements  ("WDR")  for sanitary sewer systems. The City relies on
  these programs  to protect its sewer infrastructure  from damage caused by discharges  of industrial
  waste and fats, oils, and grease. The comprehensive  management  and inspection  services provided
  by JLHA are critical for maintaining  regulatory  compliance,  minimizing  environmental  impacts,
  and safeguarding public health.

  The competitive  procurement  process  demonstrated  that JLHA  remains  the most qualified  and
  experienced  consultant  to provide  these services, given their long-standing  successful performance
  and deep understanding  of local conditions  and regulatory  requirements.  The recommended  three-
  year contract with a not-to-exceed  amount  of $194,691  reflects  a fair  and reasonable  cost to
  maintain program  continuity  and quality.

  By continuing  to leverage JLHA's  expertise,  the City can ensure effective  program  management,

  266
 timely  inspections,  enforcement  actions  when  necessary,  and ongoing  community  education  to
support  compliance.  This  approach  mitigates  risks  of  sewer  system  failures  and  associated
environmental  penalties,  ultimately  providing  cost savings  and operational  reliability  over the long
term.

BACKGROUND:  TheCityownsandoperatesasanitarysewersystemconsistingofoverll9
miles  of pipelines,  which  collects  sewage  from  residential,  commercial,  and industrial  properties
citywide.  This system must be managed  in accordance  with  state-mandated  requirements  to ensure
safe and reliable  operation.

To comply  with  the State Water  Resources  Control  Board's  2006 WDR  Order  for Sanitary  Sewer
Systems,  the City  implements  two  key programs:  the IW  Program  and FOG  Control  Program.
These  programs  regulate  facilities  that  generate  or dispose  of industrial  wastewater  and FOG,
helping  to prevent  harmful  discharges  that could  damage  the City's  sewer infrastructure  or impact
the environment.

In South  Gate,  approximately  240 active  businesses  hold  Industrial  Waste  Discharge  Permits.
These businesses  are inspected  between  one and four times  aru'iually,  depending  on the nature  of
their operations.  Permitted  businesses  are also required  to maintain  on-site  treatment  systems,  such
as grease traps or sand and grease interceptors,  to filter  harmful  substances  from  wastewater  before
discharge.  While  permits  are valid  for five years, ongoing  compliance  is monitored  through  routine
inspections  to safeguard  the integrity  of the sewer system.

The Department  of Public  Works  utilizes  the services  of an environmental  consultant  to manage
the City's  IW  and FOG  Control  Programs.  For many  years,  JLHA  has provided  consistent  and
effective  oversight  of the program  as the City's  consultant.  Their  comprehensive  support  services
include  program  management,  inspections  of  new  and  existing  commercial  and  industrial
businesses,  and enforcement  of Municipal  Code  Chapter  6.62  (Industrial  Waste).  Additionally,
they  evaluate  and  process  Industrial  Waste  reports,  review  and  approve  developer  plans,
implement  Quality  Assurance  ("QA")  procedures,  educate  the  public,  and  participate  in
community  events to promote  awareness  and compliance  with  the programs.

JLHA's  contract  recently  expired,  prompting  staff to initiate  a competitive  procurement  process
for a new  agreement.  On May  8, 2025,  a Request  for Proposal  ("RFP")  was issued  to qualified
consultants  to provide  professional  services  for  the management  of the IW  and FOG  Control
Programs.  One proposal  was received  on June 9, 2025.

On June 16, 2025,  a Selection  Committee  of City  staff  evaluated  the proposal.  The  evaluation
criteria  included  the firm's  experience;  program  understanding  and approach;  knowledge  of local,
state, and federal  laws and regulations;  and quality  control  and assurance  measures.

Based  on the Committee's  evaluation,  JLHA  is recommended  for the contract.  Under  the new
three-year  agreement,  JLHA  will  continue  to provide  the services  described  above, with  a total fee
not to exceed  $194,691.

Established  in 1985,  JLHA  is an environmental  consulting  corporation  specializing  in assisting

  267
 over  40 local  municipalities  with  water  quality  and conservation  programs.  Their  extensive
experience  includes  implementing  state  programs  for  NPDES  water  quality,  sewer  spill
prevention,  industrial  waste  and fats, oil,  and grease control,  water  conservation,  and recycling.
Their  services  include  program  administration,  planning,  reporting,  and funding.  The FOG element
of their  IW  Control  Programs  is to address  the  State Water  Board's  2006  Waste  Discharge
Requirements  Order  for  Sanitary  Sewer  Systems  ("888  WDR"),  which  includes  food  service
establishment  permitting,  FOG-oriented  inspections  and education,  and hot spot identification.

1.  Qualifications  and  Experience

1.1.  Firm  Profile

John L. Hunter  and Associates,  Inc. (JLHA) is an environmental  consulting  corporation  founded  in
1985.  We have been in business  for 40 years.  We specialize  in assisting  municipalities  implement
water  quality  and conservation  programs.  We currently  implement  elements  of these  programs
to over  40 local  municipalities.  Specific  programs  we assist  with  include  IW and  FOG Control,
NPDES,  sewer  blockage  and  spill  prevention  (including  SSMP  implementation),  stormwater
pollution  prevention,  watershed  management,  water  conservation,  and  recycling.  Services
include  program  administration,  planning,  reporting,  and  funding,  as well  as inspections,
engineering,  monitoring,  public  education,  and training.

1.2.  Relevant  Firm  Experience

Our  firm  has  been  providing  IW  and  FOG  Control  services  to  municipal  clients  since  its
incorporation  in 1985.  Prior  to the  State  Water  Board's  2006  Waste  Discharge  Requirements

Order for Sanitary Sewer Systems (555 WDRI FOGcontrol was addressed under the broad scope
of a City's  IW Control  Program,  which  was adopted  to protect  local sewer  systems.  Since 2006,
JLHA  has expanded  the  FOG element  of its IW Control  Programs  to address  the  555 WDR,
including  Food  Service  Establishment  permitting,  FOG-oriented  inspections  and education,  hot
spot  identification  and facility  prioritization.  Table 1 of this proposal  includes  a complete  list of
the IW and FOG Control  services  we provide  to current  municipal  clients,  as well  as our years  of
service.  These  services  are similar  to those  listed  in the  RFP.

We have  also assisted  six cities  update  their  SSMPs (including  Spill  Emergency  Response  Plans
formerly  OERPs), and prepare  the internal  audit  required  by the State  Water  Resources  Control
Board's  Statewide  Sanitary  Sewer  Systems  General  Order  2022-0103-DWQ  (the General  Order).
It is worth  noting  that  two  JLHA FOG clients  in the  LA area-South  Pasadena  and  Manhattan
Beach-have  received  Sewer  System  Management  Plan  (SSMP)  program  audits  by the  Los
Angeles  Regional  Water  Board.  These  audits  address  all elements  of an Enrollee's  SSMP Program,
including  FOG control  source.  In both  instances  no deficiencies  were  noted  in the  FOG Control
Program.

1.6.  Firm's Quality Assurance/Control Procedures
Our approach to the management  and implementation  of our IW/FOG Control services  is to
ensure  we  are  providing  responsive,  high-quality  services  that  are tailored  to the  needs  and
interests  of our  clients.  From  there,  our focus  is 1) determining  what  is needed  to ensure  our

clients" continued IW/FOG Control compliance, and then 2) assisting our clients  in implementing
cost-effective  solutions  to meet  or exceed  compliance  expectations.

Our team  is led by a Project  Manager.  The  Project  Manager  ensures  services  are provided  on
time,  within  the  budget,  and are of high  quality,  and also serves  as the  main  point-of-contact.
The team  is organized  so there  is more  than  one expert  ("lead")  for any task listed  in the  City's
RFP, and  that  more  than  one  team  member  can  serve  as a point-of  contact.  This  "good"
redundancy  helps  ensure  that  all services  are provided  on time,  within  the  budget,  and are of
high  quality.  Our  team  also  incorporates  multiple  levels  of review  of project  deliverables  by
qualified  team  members.  This  is done  to  provide  an unbiased  assessment  of our  accuracy,
completeness,  and  adherence  to  regulations  and  best  practices.  For example,  the  Project
Manager  will  review  and provide  internal  comment  on compliance  reports  prepared  by a Team
Lead. Both team  members  have extensive  experience  preparing  these  reports.  Another  example
is that  our Senior  field  staff  review  field  inspection  reports,  have inspectors  correct  reports  when
necessary,  and summarize  the results  to the  Project  Manager.

The  Program  Manager  and  senior  staff  meet  weekly  with  program  team  members  to discuss
program  budgets,  services  provided,  and  the  quality  of work.  These  meetings  serve  to  both
assure  continued  quality  and resolve  any issues that  may affect  the quality  of work.  We have also

developed applications to streamline and improve the QA/QC process, which  optimizes quality
of work  while  minimizing  the QA/QC expense.

We have an extensive  training  program  for our personnel.  All new personnel  are trained  generally

in our company"s approach as well as specifically in the proper implementation  of the IW/FOG
Control  services  they  will  provide.  Training  is conducted  by managers  and  senior  staff  and
continues  on a regular  basis for years.  It includes  both  hands-on  training  in the field  and in the
office.  Managers  and senior  staff  also meet  with  personnel  on a weekly  basis to continue  their
education  and to review  work  conducted  in the prior  week.

The services  we provide  are on an annual  basis,  with  many  annual  deadlines  for tasks  such  as
compliance  reports,  and field  inspections.  We  have  a proven  track  record  of providing  similar
services  to your  city-as  well  as our  many  other  municipal  clients-for  years  without  missing
these  deadlines,  and we are confident  we will  continue  to meet  them  in the coming  years.  Our
team  also  has depth  of experience  in this  work,  with  multiple  team  members  independently
capable  of providing  multiple  tasks.  This  provides  additional  assurance  that  all tasks  will  be
completed  on schedule.

  SUBJECT:  NOTICE  OF  COMPLETION  FOR  THE  HOLLYDALE  COMMUNITY
  PARK  IMPROVEMENT  PROJECT,  CITY  PROJECT  N0.  607-PRK.

  PURPOSE:  Construction  of the Hollydale  Cornrnunity  Park  Improvement  Project  ("Project")
  has been completed.  The City  of South  Gate ("City")  must formally  accept the completion  of the
  Project.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Accepting  completion  of  construction,  effective  January  31,  2025,  of  the  Hollydale
  Community  Park  Improvement,  City  Project  No.  607-PRK,  constructed  by  22
  Construction;  and
  b.  Approve  Contract  Change  Order  in the amount  of $109,495;
  c.  Appropriate  $75,000  from  Circle  Park  Project,  Account  No.  311-790-61-9217  to
  Hollydale  Community  Park Project,  Account  No. 311-790-61-9220;  and
  d.  Directing  the City  Clerk  to file  a Notice  of Completion  with  the Los Angeles  County
  Registrar  Recorder's  Office.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact  to the General  Fund.  The Project  was funded  with
  $7,129,942  in grant  and local  return  funds,  as shown  in the Budget  Summary  (See Attachment
  E).  The  final  construction  contract  amount  is  $2,003,983,  which  is  inclusive  of  (a)  the
  $2,001,372  contract  amount,  (b) an increase  of $109,495,  (c) and the reconciliation  of quantities
  of $106,885.  The net construction  cost is $2,003,983.

  ANALYSIS:  Construction  of the Project  was  substantially  completed  on January  31, 2025.
  There  were  no Stop Notices  against  the project.  As  such, based  on the Public  Contract  Code
  section  7107,  staff  has prepared  and released  the final  payment  of the 5% retention  held  from
  construction  invoice  payments  to 22  Construction  since  it has been  more  than  60 days  of
  cessation  of work  on the project.

  BACKGROUND:  The  Project  is included  in the Fiscal  Year  2024/25  Capital  Improvement
  Program  ("CIP")  and was programmed  to support  the renovation  of the park.  Improvements
  completed  as part of the Project  include  a new 1,700-square-foot  building,  a rubberized  walking
  path,  synthetic  turf,  a movie  screen,  a new  irrigation  system,  and  updated  landscaping.
  Additional  enhancements  consist  of a new  basketball  court,  two  shade  structures  with  pi,cnic

  1
  308
 areas, and a new  wrought  iron  perimeter  fence  to the east and an 8-foot-high  block  wall  to the
west.  The  Project  also features  a subsurface  water  chamber  designed  to capture  and recharge
rainwater.

These  upgrades  significantly  enhance  recreational  opportunities  for  residents,  improve  the
overall  quality  of life  in the community,  and support  healthier  lifestyles.  In addition,  the use of
synthetic  turf,  drought-tolerant  landscaping,  and  efficient  irrigation  systems  will  help  reduce
long-term  maintenance  and water  costs for the City.

On  August  27,  2024,  the  City  Council  approved  Contract  No.  2024-68-CC  with  22
Construction,  for  the re-renovation  of the Hollydale  Community  Park,  City  Project  No.  607-
PRK,  in an amount  not-to-exceed  $2,001,372.  Construction  began on September  16, 2024,  and it
was completed  on January  31, 2025.

One contract  change  order in the amount  of $109,495  was approved  administratively  to complete
necessary  work  at the  park.  This  included  restoring  landscaping,  repairing  drainage  issues,
adding  decorative  stonework,  installing  a new  chain  link  fence between  the north  wall  and the
existing  building,  adding  lighting  and  electrical  work,  and  completing  other  minor
improvements.  A full  list of these items  is provided  in the Change  Order  Log.

The final  construction  cost of Hollydale  Community  Park was $2,003,983.

The  contractor  has  successfully  fulfilled  all  contract  obligations,  completing  the  project  in
accordance  with  the approved  plans  and specifications.  The work  was performed  with  quality
craftsmanship,  delivered  within  budget,  and  completed  on  schedule.  Final  inspections  have
confirmed  that all improvements  meet the required  standards.

With  the project  now  complete  and all contract  requirements  satisfied,  the City  Council  is in a
position  to formally  accept  the project  and authorize  the filing  of the Notice  of Completion  with
the Los Angeles  County  Registrar-Recorder's  Office.

SUBJECT:  AGREEMENT  WITH  KIMLEY-HORN  TO  PROVIDE  PROFESSIONAL
ENVIRONMENT  AL  CONSULTING  SERVICES,  AND  REIMBURSEMENT  AGREEMENT
WITH  J.B.  HUNT  TRANSPORT,  INC.  TO  PAY  FOR  COSTS  FOR  A PROJECT  AT  5440,  5532,
AND  5625 SOUTHERN  AVENUE

PURPOSE:  To approve  a professional  environmental  consulting  services  contract  with  Kimley-Horn  for
preparation  of environmental  documentation  for  a project  to develop  an operations  center  with  truck
parking  on three properties  totaling  23.61  acres located  at 5440,  5532,  and 5625  Southern  Avenue,  and
approve  a reimbursement  agreement  with  the applicant,  J.B. Hunt  Transport,  Inc. to pay for  costs.  The
proposed  project  will  develop  the northern  property  for truck  parking  during  the first phase, and redevelop
the southern  properties  to serve as the West Coast Operations  Center headquarters  during  the second phase.
It should be noted that the proposed project  is not under  consideration,  but only  the contracts  needed  to
begin the environmental  documentation.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:

a.  Approving  the Professional  Services  Agreement  with  Kimley-Horn  to provide  on-call  environmental
  consulting  services;
b.  Approving  a Reimbursement  Agreement  with  J.B. Hunt  Transport,  Inc.;
c.  Authorizing  the use of Purchase  orders  in directing  work;  and
d.  Authorizing  the Mayor  to execute  the Agreements  in a form  acceptable  to the City  Attorney.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact  as the applicant  is responsible  for paying  the City  of Sout
Gate's  ("City")  consultant's  costs and administrative  costs.

ANALYSIS:  The Plaru'iing  Division  of the Community  Development  Department  requires  the use of
consultants  to assist with  environmental  services  that are either  beyond  the capacity  of plaru'iing  staff due
to the scope of a project  or when the project  analysis  requires  special  expertise.

Kimley-Horn  is part of the City's  environmental  consulting  "bench"  which  is a list of three  consultants
the City  contracted  with  in June 2022 to provide  on-call  environmental  services.  Staff reached  out to the
bench  consultants  about  the need  for  environmental  services  for  the proposed  project  and received  a
proposal  from  Kimley-Horn,  which  was found  acceptable  by staff and the applicant.

The applicant  is responsible  for paying  the cost of the City's  consultant  for work  on the applicant's  project
and staff time.  For an environmental  impact  report  ("EIR"),  the payment  covers "Consultant's  Fee plus
25% Admin  Fee."  Typically,  a deposit  is made  by the applicant  to the City  for the amount  identified  in
the consultant's  proposal,  plus 25% as required  in the City's  Fee Schedule.  1

  317
 In this case, the applicant  is ready and willing  to reimburse  the City for any and all costs incurred  by staff
related to the review  of the environmental  documents.  However,  the applicant  is requesting  to put the
necessary  amoiu'it  on deposit  to be drawn  down  and invoiced  based on actual  staff costs (e.g., hours
worked).  The reimbursement  agreement  provides  for a deposit of the full amount of all funds required  by
the City:  Kimley-Horn's  costs and administrative  costs for staff time.  The agreement  makes clear the
amounts are deposits that should be drawn upon as actual work is expended by Kimley-Horn  and the City.
The applicant  contends  that a flat  fee based  solely  on 25%  of Kimley-Horn's  costs would  not be
appropriate  under the Mitigation  Fee Act, which prohibits  local agencies from charging  fees for filing  and
processing applications that exceed the estimated reasonable cost of providing  the service for which  the
fee is charged. Government  Code § 66014(a) reads as follows:

  (a) Notwithstanding  any other provision  of law, when  a local  agency  charges  fees for zoning
  variances;  zoning  changes;  use permits;  building  inspections;  building  permits;  filing  and
  processing  applications  and petitions  filed  with  the local  agency  formation  commission  or
  conducting  preliminary  proceedings  or proceedings  under  the Cortese-Knox-Hertzberg  Local
  Government  Reorganization  Act of 2000, Division  3 (cornmencing  with  Section  56000)  of Title
  5; the processing  of maps  under  the provisions  of the  Subdivision  Map  Act,  Division  2
  (commencing  with Section  66410) of Title  7; or planning  services under the authority  of Chapter
  3 (cornmencing  with  Section  65100)  of Division  1 of Title  7 or under any other authority;
  fees may not exceed the estimated  reasonable  cost of providing  the service  for which  the fee
  is charged,  unless a question  regarding  the amount  of the fee charged in excess of the estimated
  reasonable  cost of providing  the services or materials  is submitted  to, and approyed  by, a popular
  vote of two-thirds of those electorsvoting on the issue.{Emphasisaddedl

The applicant  argues that imposing  a flat fee for CEQA  review  based solely on the total dollar value of a
contract  is not reasonably  related to the cost of the services provided  by staff. Simply  put, the contracted
price for preparation  of the environmental  document  by Kimley-Horn  does not determine  or relate to the
level  of staff service  required  and is reimbursable  in connection  with  the processing  of an EIR  for a
project.  The fee for City staff services should be totaled separately  and based on a metric  that reasonably
reflects  the degree of services provided.  The proposed  reimbursement  agreement  remedies  this issue  by
basing staff's  costs on a rate of $155 per hour, which  is the hourly  rate for a senior planner.

City Council  should keep in mind that other applicants  have been charged the 25% administrative  fee as
required.  The proposed  reimbursement  agreement  would  set a precedence  in which  staff would  monitor
its time  for billing  purposes  and the City  would  have to refund  the applicant  for any unused  funds
remaining  in the deposit.  Alternatively,  City  Council  could deny the reimbursement  agreement  and the
applicant  would  still have to pay the costs based on the fee listed in the City's  adopted Fee Schedule.  Per
Section 11.51.100  of the South Gate Municipal  Code, all filing  fees established  by the City shall be paid
upon the filing  of an application. Thus, ifthe  fee is not paid, staff will not begin work onthe environmental
documentation  needed for the project.

118 trucks,  and 203 trailers.

legally  defensible  EIR that  fully  analyzes  and discloses  any and all impacts  associated  with  the  proposed
Project.

A. APPROACH  AND SCOPE OF WORK

Project  Approach

Kimley-Horn"s  strategy  for the  planning  and environmental  process  begins  with  reviewing  available
project  documentation,  and reviewing  any technical  studies  that  have been prepared  for the project.
Building  on this, our project  team will prepare  environmental  analyses to create a thorough,  complete
administrative  and technical  record  upon  which  new  conclusions  will  be based. Many  projects  will
consider  a complex  set of issues and concerns  while  balancing  community,  business, and public agency
interests  within  the  boundaries  of the regulatory  review  process  and procedures.  Such complexities
require  creativity,  extensive  hands-on  experience,  and a commitment  to carefully  manage the project  to
successful  completion  despite  obstacles  that  may arise. This effort  will require  active  participation  and
the application  of a team approach  from start to finish. Our team will facilitate  and develop a collaborative
process that will result in the successful  completion  ofthe  EIR.

Scope  of Services

Kimley-Horn  will provide  the services specifically  set forth  below. The following  Scope of Services assumes
the baseline conditions,  Project  Description,  and approach  will not change, once approved  by the City. It
is also assumed the City will provide  one reconciled  set of comments  for each deliverable,  and that the
comments  will not raise new substantive  issues requiring  re-analysis.

The Scope of Services detailed  below details the tasks necessary to successfully  complete  CEQA compliance
for the proposed  Project.

TASK 1  PROJECT  INITIATION

1.1  Kick-Off  Meeting

This Task includes a Kick-OffMeeting with the City to discussthe CEQAProiect in greater detail. This initial
meeting  is a key milestone,  which  is vital to the Project's  success and CEQA compliance.  The primary
objectives will be to confirm the City's expectations and Project  goals, and  develop/refine the  Project
Description.  The analysis'  parameters,  construction  details,  buildout  conditions,  scheduling,  and overall
communications  protocol  will also be established.  Prior to the meeting,  Kimley-Horn  will distribute  a
Kick-Off Meeting  Agenda and Data Needs Technical  Memorandum  (TM).

1.2  Data Review  and Site Reconnaissance

Kimley-Horn  will conduct  reconnaissance  of the project  site and surrounding  area. We will review  readily
available  project  materials  and reference  data, including  planning and policy documentation  from the City
and any other agencies affected  by the Project.  Kimley-Horn  will assess whether  available  information  is
adequate  and complete.  The City will be notified  if additional  information  is needed in order to complete
the  data  collection.  Data  obtained  through  this  task  will  be foundational  to  the  environmental
documentation  and incorporated  into the analysis, as appropriate.

1.3  Project  Description

The project  description  is a critical  component  because  it is the basis for the environmental  analysis.  Based
on information  provided  by the City, Kimley-Horn  will prepare  a Draft  Project  Description  for City review
and approval.  The Project  Description  will detail  the Project's  location,  environmental  setting,  background

and history, project characteristics, construction schedule/phasing, and discretionary  actions.  Exhibits  will
be  prepared  to  depict  the  regional  and  site  vicinity  and  key  project  components  to  support  the
environmental  analyses.  Kimley-Horn  will respond  to one reconciled  set of comments  on the Draft  Project
Description.  We will prepare  a "check  copy"  Project  Description  and submit  to the City for approval  prior
to finalizing.

1.4  Notice  of Preparation

Kimley-Horn  will prepare  a Notice  of Preparation  (NOP) for the project  and submit  it to the City for review.
Kimley-Horn  will  respond  to  one  consolidated  set  of  City  comments  on  the  Administrative  NOP.
Kimley-Horn  will prepare  a check copy of the NOP and submit  to the City (along with  a redline  copy of the
Administrative  NOP) for approval  prior  to public  release.  This Task assumes  the Project  Description  will
not change  and the comments  will not raise new substantive  issues requiring  re-analysis.

1.5  Scoping  Meeting

A Public  Scoping  Meeting  will be scheduled  during  the Notice  of Preparation  (NOP) public  review  period
to orient  the  community  on CEQA"s intent  and review  processes,  and the  environmental  issues  to be
addressed  in the  EIR. The Public  Scoping  Meeting  will  also enable  the  community  to understand  the
Project  and comment  on environmental  concerns.  It is assumed  that  the  City will  provide  a meeting
location  and facilitate  coordination.  Kimley-Horn  will  provide  graphics  to supplement  a presentation  to
the public,  as appropriate.  Following  the presentation,  the meeting  will be devoted  to public  participation,

3.5  Mitigation  Monitoring  and  Reporting  Program

To comply  with  the CEQA Guidelines  Section  21081.6,  Kimley-Horn  will prepare  a Mitigation  Monitoring

to identify  appropriate  monitoring  steps/procedures and to provide  a basis for monitoring  such measures
during  and upon  project  implementation.  The MMRP  will  be created  in a tabular  checklist  format  that
indicates  those  mitigation  measures  identified  in  the  EIR,  the  monitoring  milestone  (at  what

agency/department  responsible for verifying implementation  of the  measure),  and  the  method  of
verification  (such as documentation  or field checks).

The MMRP  will  be prepared  pursuant  to Public  Resources  Code  Section  21081.6.  For each  mitigation
measure  contained  in the EIR, the MMRP  will identify:  the party or parties  responsible  forimplementation
(individuals,  departments);  timeframe  and mechanism  for monitoring;  funding  source(s);  and monitoring
and performance  criteria  (to measure  success of mitigation).  The MMRP  will be bound  separately  for use
as an independent  document  for field  verification  of adequate  implementation  of mitigation  measures
and any remedial  action  necessary  to achieve  adequate  mitigation.

To the extent  feasible,  Kimley-Horn  will tie mitigation  measures  directly  to required  authorizations  (e.g.,
grading  and building  permits,  etc.).  Revisions  will be made to the MMRP  as directed  by the City following
internal  review  of the AFEIR.

PURPOSE:  To approve  the use of the CTFGP  funds in the amount  of $100, 000 for overtime  and
equipment.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Authorizing  utilization  of the 2025-2026  Cannabis  Tax fund  Grant  Program  ("CTFGP")
  Funds  in the amount  of $100,000 for overtime  and equipment;
  b.  Amending  the  Fiscal  Year  2025/26  Law  Enforcement  Grants  Fund  Budget  by
  appropriating  $16,000 for overtime  salaries  and $86,000 for equipment;  and
  c.  Authorizing  the Chief  of Police  or his designee  to execute  the CTFGP  Agreement  in a form
  acceptable  to the City  Attorney.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact  to the General  Fund  and no requirement  for the
City  of South  Gate ("City")  to match  the grant funds.  The total  amount  of funding  that has been
allocated  to the City  for FY 2025/26  is $100,000.

ANALYSIS:  The South  Gate Police  Department  submitted  a grant  application  to the California
Highway  Patrol  Cannabis  Tax Fund  Grand  Program  in early  2025.  In June 2025,  the California
Highway  Patrol  awarded  the South Gate Police  Department  $100,000  for overtime  and equipment.

BACKGROTJND:  With  the passage  of Proposition  64, the Control,  Regulate,  and Tax Adult  Use
of Marijuana  Act  ("AUMA"),  California  voters  mandated  the  state  set aside  funding  for  the
California  Highway  Patrol  ("CHP")  to award  grants  to local  governments  and qualified  nonprofit
organizations,  as described  in Revenue  and Taxation  Code Section  34019(f)(3)(B).

The CTFGP  marks  an important  step toward  reducing  impaired  driving  crashes,  increasing  public
awareness  surrounding  the dangers  of impaired  driving,  and making  California's  roadways  a safer
place to travel.

The  CHP  works  closely  with  state and local  agencies  and other  traffic  safety  stakeholders  to
actively  address  impaired  driving.  The  CHP  will  consider  a variety  of factors  in determining

  354
 specific  needs for each grant cycle,  including  opportunities  and projects  best suited to prevent  the
loss of life,  injuries,  and property  damage  caused by driving  under the influence  of alcohol  and/or
drugs.

The funding  provided  is appropriated  by the California  State Controller's  Office,  and all grants are
awarded  on  a  competitive  basis,  unless  otherwise  specified  within  the  Request  for
Application.  The CHP  may consider  an extended  project  performance  period  based on need, as
determined  by the CHP.  The awarding  of a grant does not guarantee  ongoing  or future  funding.

Project  Description
The South Gate  Police Department  (SGPD)  has seen a steady rise in collisions caused by intoxicated  drivers.
This is according  to statistical data involving  alcohol and drugs since the legalization  of marijuana.  The SGPD
impaired driving enforcement project strategy consists of three points: Training, Education,  and enforcement.
The SGPD Project will promote increased public awareness  of the dangers of driving under the influence of
alcohol, drugs, and marijuana.  Enforcement  of D.U.I. laws per(aining to driving  under the influence of alcohol,
drugs, marijuana,  and other associated  collision factors will reduce the number  of citizens killed or injured in
collisions.

Through the SGPD's impaired driving enforcement  project, we will enhance  public safety and aim to reduce
the number of persons killed or injured in collisions  involving alcohol, drugs,  and marijuana.  The SGPD will
partner with the Automobile  Club Of Southern California to distribute informative  safety material to drivers of
all ages about the effects of alcohol, drugs, and marijuana  on driving. The SGPD will utilize social media and
community  presentations  to heighten awareness.  Project funds will be used for D.U.I. saturation  patrol
overtime salaries and a dedicated  D.U.I. enforcement  vehicle to carry out enforcement  efforts.

The SGPD  will also provide  police  officers  the needed  training  to recognize  the signs and symptoms  of
impairment  (SFST, ARIDE, and DRE). Funds will be used to train additional  police officers to recognize  the
signs and symptoms  of impairment  for DUI investigations.  Community  outreach can be accomplished
through social media outreach to highlight awareness  and purchase equipment  to support our DUI
enforcement  and prosecution  efforts.

Through the SGPD impaired driving education  and enforcement  project, police officers will gain proper
training and experience  in identifying drivers under the influence of alcohol, drugs, and marijuana.  By
accomplishing  this we are able to better serve our communities  as we improve public safety.

Problem  Statement  & Proposed  Solution
The South Gate Police Department  (SGPD) is facing a significant public safety crisis stemming from an
increase in impaired driving incidents and the abuse of cannabis within the community.  Between 2020 and
2024, DUI-related  collisions accounted  for 480 incidents, making up nearly 1 0% of the 5,049 reported
collisions in this timeframe. Furthermore,  of the 27 fatal collisions  recorded  during  this period,  4 (nearly  1 5%)
were directly linked to impaired driving.

Despite  a decline  in DUI-related  collisions  in 2024 (80 incidents,  down from 138 in 2023),  impaired  driving
continues  to be a pressing issue. SGPD's challenges  are exacerbated  by staffing shortages and high turnover
rates, which have necessitated  the hiring and training  of new officers,  many of whom lack experience  in
identifying  and investigating  impaired  driving.  These  staffing  constraints  hinder  the department's  ability  to
provide  critical training, such as Standardized  Field Sobriety  Test (SFST) and Advanced  Roadside  Impaired
Driving  Enforcement  (ARIDE) certifications, and to maintain  robust enforcement measures.

In addition, the community  is grappling with a rise in cannabis abuse, particularly  among juveniles.  SGPD has
made multiple arrests related to the illegal sale of cannabis vape pens near middle and high schools. These
investigations  have uncovered  links to other criminal activities, such as possession  of stolen vehicles and
weapons.  The increased  use of cannabis products among  juveniles  has resulted in unsafe behaviors,
including impaired operation of bicycles, e-bikes, scooters,  skateboards,  pocket bikes, and vehicles, further
endangering  public safety.

This multifaceted  issue highlights  the urgent  need for community  education,  enhanced  officer  training,  and
increased  enforcement efforts to address impaired driving and cannabis  abuse.  Without  strategic  intervention
the safety  of SGPD's community  will continue to be at risk.

Solution:
Having additional  officers on the roadways who can enforce traffic-related  matters, with specialized  training in
DUI investigations,  serves as an asset to our community.  This increases the number of officers available to
handle DUI investigations,  facilitating more efficient investigations,  thorough documentation  through report
writing leading to convictions  and arrests. It will also promote a heightened  awareness  of zero-tolerance
enforcement  for DUI/DUID  traffic violations and collisions,  enhancing  proactive  traffic  enforcement  to reduce
DUI/DUID  incidents within  the SGPD jurisdiction.

The SGPD  seeks  to enhance  its enforcement  efforts  by utilizing  additional  officers  trained  in DUI
investigations to compliment  the enforcement  efforts of the SGPD  traffic bureau. SGPD plans to conduct 8
DUI saturation  enforcement  operations  throughout  the grant year,  specifically  targeting impaired drivers to
reduce injuries and fatal collisions. These enforcement  operations  will supplement  the existing patrol force
and focus on areas within the jurisdiction  of SGPD.

Officers assigned to DUI/DUID  enforcement  will work in two-person teams with enforcement  operations
primarily taking place during the evening/nighttime  hours. SGPD plans to conduct 8 saturation  patrols (2 per
quarter), each lasting a minimum of 8 hours. These efforts aim to reduce DUI-related  deaths and collisions,
ultimately  improving roadway safety in the community.

Additionally,  SGPD seeks funding to acquire a dedicated  DUI Enforcement  Vehicle to support these efforts.
This vehicle will be a marked "DUI Enforcement"  unit equipped to assist officers in locating and apprehending
impaired drivers and addressing  primary collision factors such as speeding,  unsafe turning, and failure to
yield. The vehicle will be utilized during enforcement  operations  to ensure effective and efficient targeting of
DUI/DUID  incidents and to reduce related collisions and fatalities.

Through these measures,  SGPD aims to improve  roadway safety, reduce  DUI-related  incidents  and fatalities

Performance  Measures/Scope  of Work
The South  Gate Police  Department  (SGPD)  Impaired  Driving  Enforcement  Grant aims to save lives and
ensure  the long-term  benefits  of its efforts.  By increasing  public  awareness  and implementing  targeted
enforcement,  the SGPD  seeks  to achieve  a IO% reduction  in both DUI-related  incidents  and fatal collisions.

To achieve  this goal, the SGPD will conduct 8 DUI enforcement  operations  throughout  the grant year with 2
per quarter  (every three months). These operations  will focus on identifying  and apprehending  impaired
drivers to reduce injuries and fatalities. Officers involved in these operations  will utilize specialized training,
including Standardized  Field Sobriety Test (SFST) and Advanced  Roadside  Impaired Driving Enforcement
(ARIDE) techniques,  to conduct thorough  DUI/DUID  investigations.

Overtime  salaries  will support  these  operations,  with each detail  involving  a single  vehicle  staffed  by two
officers to ensure safety and efficiency.  These enforcement  efforts will primarily occur during nighttime hours
or other high-risk periods for impaired driving, with each operation  lasting eight hours. The goal is to conduct
two enforcement  operations  per quarter throughout  the grant period.

A dedicated  marked "DUI Enforcement"  vehicle will facilitate these efforts. This vehicle will allow officers to
effectively locate and apprehend  impaired drivers while addressing  key collision factors such as speeding,
unsafe turning movements,  and failure to yield. By providing officers with the tools necessary  for targeted
enforcement,  the vehicle will enhance the department's  ability  to reduce  DUI-related  incidents  and fatalities
while reinforcing  its commitment  to community safety.

Project Performance  Evaluation
The South Gate Police Department (SGPD) will analyze data collected during the grant term to complete a
final evaluation in the fourth and final quarter of the project. This evaluation will summarize the grant's
accomplishments,  challenges, and key activities. It will also include an assessment of whether the goals and
objectives were met, exceeded, or, if not achieved, an explanation as to why.

The SGPD will use Crossroads Analytics Software and in-house RMS soffware to track collision and
enforcement data. This data will allow for comparisons between the grant year and previous years, helping to
identify trends and assess the grant's potential impact. Statistics on DUI arrests, DUI-related traffic collisions,
injury-related DUI collisions, and DUI traffic fatalities will also be compiled for quarterly evaluations.

Program Sustainability
The South Gate Police Department (SGPD) is committed to reducing reliance on future grant funding by
building sustainable enforcement and prevention capabilities within its traffic division. As staffing levels
improve, the department's long-term plan is to fully staff the traffic division with two motor officers, two DUI
enforcement vehicles, and eight community service officers. A fully staffed traffic division will enable SGPD to
conduct consistent and proactive DUI enforcement efforts without the need for external funding.

With these resources in place, the traffic division will be able to focus on targeted enforcement strategies,
such as saturation patrols, sobriety checkpoints, and community outreach programs, ensuring continued
efforts to reduce DUI-related incidents and fatalities. Additionally, community service officers will play a crucial
role in supporting non-enforcement  duties, allowing sworn officers to dedicate more time to DUI enforcement.

The timeline for achieving this objective is directly tied to improvements  in staffing levels. As recruitment and
retention strategies take effect, the SGPD anticipates incremental progress over the next three to five years.
During this period, the department will prioritize internal training for officers, ensuring they are equipped with
the skills necessary to maintain and expand DUI enforcement efforts independently of grant funding.

This transition plan emphasizes self-sufficiency while maintaining a focus on roadway safety, ensuring  the
community continues to benefit from effective DUI enforcement and prevention measures even in the
absence of significant grant support.

Administrative  Support
The South Gate Police Department (SGPD) has extensive experience successfully managing various grants,
even amidst challenges such as a reduction in police personnel. The department has consistently maintained
accurate record-keeping,  data entry, and statistical reporting to ensure the success of its grant-funded
projects. SGPD has efficiently handled the processing of all financial records and will continue to manage and
retain records for the Office of Traffic Safety (OTS), Alcohol Beverage Control (ABC) and any other entity we
enter into an agreement with.

With a dedicated and motivated staff, the SGPD is well-prepared  to undertake the tasks necessary to reduce
DUI incidents and enhance public safety within the community. The department's  personnel and physical
resources are well-suited to implement the project effectively and achieve its objectives.

  control.  Together,  property  and sales taxes  form  the backbone  of our

  City  Manager  Houston  stated tonight's  public  hearing  and presentation  of
  the budget  for the coming  fiscal  year. There  was a presentation  given  at
  the first  meeting  in June which  highlighted  the core pieces of the budget,
  operations  and accomplishments  from  last year.

  City  Manager  Houston  asked Mr. Frausto,  Director  of Administrative
  Services,  to start the presentation.

  Mr. Frausto  presented  the Fiscal  Year 2025/26  Proposed  Budget  for
  adoption.  Mr. Frausto  deferred  to a couple  of department  heads to speak
  about some of the growth  and costs the city has experienced  over the last
  several  years.

  Chief  of Police  Arakawa  gave his presentation.

  Steve Costley,  Director  of Parks & Recreation,  gave his presentation.

  Arturo  Cervantes,  Director  of Public  Works,  gave his presentation.

  Mr. Houston  spoke on the options  the city is facing,  details  on those
  options  and a recommendation  approach  for this yeais  budget.

  Council  Member  Hurtado  explained  that freezing  positions  are also
  freezing  services.  He met with  the directors  and discussed  their budgets.

  overtime.  Implementing  a temporary  hiring  freeze  for non-critical
  positions.  Review  overtime  usage in all departments.  Reassigning  staff

  approved  today  and all proposed  cuts.

  significant  amount  of profit  to pay for their event.

  Mayor  Davila  believes  the city can do without  the carnival  during  the
  fourth  of July event.

  Mr. Costley  informed  City  Council  that the carnival  is the moneymaker  for
